cards.back: A metric that measures the amount of resources (such as time and memory) required to execute an algorithm as a function of the input size.
A function bundled together with references to its surrounding state, allowing it to access variables from an outer function even after that outer function has finished executing.
A property of certain operations in mathematics and computer science whereby they can be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the initial application.
The provision of a single interface to entities of different types, or the use of a single symbol to represent multiple different types.
A method of solving a problem where the solution depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem.
The ability of different parts or blocks of a program to be executed out-of-order or in partial order without affecting the final outcome.
An optimization technique used primarily to speed up computer programs by storing the results of expensive function calls and returning the cached result when the same inputs occur again.
The act of changing an object's state or value after it has been created, often contrasted with immutable data structures.
The process of translating a data structure or object state into a format that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later.
A technique used to limit the rate at which a function can fire, ensuring it only executes once over a specified time interval.
